title: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 72-78 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 46-47)
source: Nag Hammadi Codex II page photographs (Claremont Colleges Digital Library, Nag Hammadi Archive) + Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley (CC BY 4.0) + English by Mark M. Mattison (public domain)
description: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 72-78, in the Coptic of Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 46-47, with each saying linked to the photograph of the papyrus page and an English translation.
introduction:
The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, introduced as the hidden sayings written down by Didymos Judas Thomas. The only complete copy is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, a papyrus book in Coptic copied in the 4th century and found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945; it is now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo (inv. 10544). Greek fragments of the work survive in three Oxyrhynchus papyri (P. Oxy. 1, 654 and 655), which are not shown here.

This entry covers the sayings 72-78, which begin on codex page 46; the end of saying 78 is on page 47. The Coptic is given line by line; the small numbers are codex page and line (for example 33.5), so each line can be found on the photograph. Page and line breaks follow the Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley, which he made from the photographs of The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices, the negatives shown here.

Photograph: Codex II page 46, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 56, CCDL nha 2870; Nag Hammadi Archive of the Institute for Antiquity and Christianity, Claremont Colleges Digital Library. Checked on the photograph: page 46 line 1 begins '[ⲡⲉ]ϫ̣ⲉ̣ⲟ̣ⲩ̣ⲣ̣[ⲱⲙ]ⲉ̣ ⲛ̣ⲁ̣ϥ̣ ̣ϫ̣ⲉϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲥⲛⲏⲩ' and line 32 reads 'ⲛ̄[ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧ]ⲛ̣ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲟⲩ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲉⲅⲓ' (the beginnings of the first and last lines are damaged; the page ends with ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲉⲅⲓ, continued as ⲥⲧⲁⲛⲟⲥ on page 47).
translator_notes: Coptic: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition (Paul C. Dilley), version 6.2.0, CC BY 4.0, shown in the manuscript's own spelling with words grouped as bound groups. Editorial signs are the edition's: square brackets mark letters lost in a gap (restored by the editor, or dots for the number of lost letters), a dot under a letter marks an uncertain reading, round brackets write out a letter abbreviated by a stroke at a line end, angle brackets mark letters added by the editor, curly brackets letters the editor removes, double square brackets letters erased by the scribe.

The small numbers in the Coptic are codex page and line (page.line) as marked in the edition. Where a word is divided between two lines on the papyrus, the edition sometimes keeps the word whole on one line, so a line can begin a few letters earlier or later on the photograph (for example 39.33-34, and the page change inside saying 13).

English: Mark M. Mattison, The Gospel of Thomas (public domain). Mattison's symbols: [ ] gap in the text, ( ) editorial insertion, / \ editorial correction of a scribal error. The saying headings are his.
Saying 75: Mattison renders monachos as 'one'; it is usually translated 'single', 'solitary' or 'alone'.

[Someone said to him], "Tell my brothers to divide our inheritance with me."

He said to him, "Who made me a divider?"

He turned to his disciples and said to them, "Am I really a divider?"

translation.text:
Jesus said, "The Father's kingdom can be compared to a merchant with merchandise who found a pearl. The merchant was wise; they sold their merchandise and bought that single pearl for themselves.

"You, too, look for the treasure that doesn't perish but endures, where no moths come to eat and no worms destroy."
translation.scan_note: On page 46 lines 13-22 (Codex II page 46, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 56, CCDL nha 2870). Opens 'ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉ' at 46.13; ends 'ⲉⲟⲩⲱⲙ⳿ ⲟⲩⲇⲉ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥϥⲛ︤ⲧ︥ ⲧⲁⲕⲟ' at 46.22. Jesus said, "I'm the light that's over all. I am the All. The All has come from me and unfolds toward me.

"Split a log; I'm there. Lift the stone, and you'll find me there."
